content: Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from infectious diseases worldwide. The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine is currently the only available vaccine for tuberculosis, but its protective efficacy is incomplete and varies significantly. The modified Vaccinia Ankara virus expressing antigen 85A (MVA85A) is a viral vector vaccine developed to enhance the protective effects of BCG and prevent tuberculosis. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of the MVA85A vaccine as a booster to BCG in humans. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, WHO ICTRP, and ClinicalTrials.gov, with searches completed by May 10, 2018. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving MVA85A administered with BCG were included, regardless of participants' age or HIV status. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and risk of bias of the trials and extracted data for analysis. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of active tuberculosis. Dichotomous outcomes were summarized using risk ratios (RR) and risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Meta-analyses were performed when appropriate, and narrative summaries were provided when meta-analysis was not feasible. The search identified six studies related to four Phase 2 RCTs, enrolling a total of 3838 participants. These trials were funded by government agencies, charities, and philanthropic organizations. Five studies included infants, one of which involved infants born to HIV-positive mothers, while one study included adults living with HIV. All trials involved researchers from Oxford University, who were instrumental in the vaccine's laboratory development. In some studies, participants received intradermal MVA85A after BCG vaccination, while in others, HIV-exposed infants received MVA85A before selective deferred BCG vaccination. The largest trial, conducted in 2797 African children, was well-designed and had a low risk of bias for most parameters. However, there was uncertainty regarding selective reporting bias, as no precise case definition endpoints for active tuberculosis were published before the trial analysis. The addition of MVA85A to BCG likely has no significant effect on the risk of developing microbiologically confirmed tuberculosis (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.62; 3439 participants, 2 trials; moderate-certainty evidence) or on the risk of initiating tuberculosis treatment (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.33; 3687 participants, 3 trials; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, MVA85A likely does not affect the risk of developing latent tuberculosis (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.21; 3831 participants, 4 trials; moderate-certainty evidence). The safety profile of MVA85A was favorable, with no evidence of life-threatening serious adverse effects (RD 0.00, 95% CI –0.00 to 0.00; 3692 participants, 3 trials; high-certainty evidence). However, vaccination with MVA85A was probably associated with an increased risk of local skin reactions at the injection site (3187 participants, 3 trials; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of an increased risk of systemic adverse effects related to vaccination (144 participants, 1 trial; low-certainty evidence). These findings are consistent with Phase 1 studies, which reported transient, superficial injection site reactions and mild, short-lived symptoms such as malaise and fever. In conclusion, intradermal administration of MVA85A in addition to BCG is safe but does not appear to be effective in reducing the risk of developing tuberculosis.
